meta.case_name: A Mobile Telecom Company in UK

prompt.context: In 2006, a UK mobile telecom company (Company A) tried to build a relationship with a fixed line telecom operator (Company B) to provide their customers with 3G broadband data service. At that time, 3G was not common.
prompt.question: What types of partnership structures should Company A consider when partnering with Company B? List the pros and cons of each, and identify other factors that would determine the optimal partnership structure. What would you need to know to select the ideal partnership, and what kind of partnership do you think would be best?

clarifying_info.q: Can Company A develop 3G technology using their own R&D? What are the challenges?
clarifying_info.a: This is a question you should explore — the interviewer will probe your thinking on this.

clarifying_info.q: Does Company B have any patents on their 3G technology? Are there competitors with similar technology?
clarifying_info.a: This is a question you should explore — the interviewer will probe your thinking on this.

clarifying_info.q: Are there synergies Company A can expect beyond just implementing the 3G technology after the partnership?
clarifying_info.a: The scope of the partnership with Company B is not going to be beyond the usage of their 3G technology.

clarifying_info.q: What is the geographical area of business for Company A and Company B?
clarifying_info.a: This is a question you should explore — the interviewer will probe your thinking on this.

clarifying_info.q: What is the demand for 3G mobile broadband data service? Is it growing?
clarifying_info.a: This is a question you should explore — the interviewer will probe your thinking on this.

framework: Define the three partnership structure types to evaluate: M&A, Joint Venture (JV), and Business Alliance
For each structure, list pros and cons systematically

Identify key information needed to determine the optimal structure (Company A's own R&D capability, Company B's technology attractiveness/patents, potential synergies, geographic overlap, market demand for 3G)
Apply the information gathered to select the best partnership type
For Part 2: quantify the financial impact of launching free 3G service and assess feasibility

questions.prompt: What are the pros and cons of each of the three partnership structures (M&A, JV, Business Alliance)?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers all three structures with balanced pros/cons: (1) M&A — pro: more control; cons: not flexible, requires strict due diligence, high cost, overlap of business and back-end functions. (2) JV — pro: can combine each company's strengths to create a specific new business; con: if the scope of synergy is limited, a JV may not be preferable. (3) Business Alliance — pro: flexible, pay fee only per usage; con: difficult to control the partner, especially for customized service arrangements.

questions.prompt: Given that the scope of the partnership with Company B will not extend beyond the usage of their 3G technology, which partnership structure is best?
questions.guidance: Since Company A cannot pursue synergies beyond the initial 3G use, a Business Alliance is preferable. Company A can start by paying the usage fee. If additional synergies arise in the future, other options (JV or M&A) can be reconsidered. An excellent candidate will note that synergies from overlapping business and geographical areas are important when considering M&A, and that JVs carry legal complexity.

questions.prompt: Company C (a competitor of Company A) is going to begin providing 3G broadband mobile service for free to its existing customers. If Company A starts a similar free service, the initial CAPEX will be $1,080M, and Company A wants to recover this investment within 3 years. Company A's monthly cost per customer will increase by $5 (from $15 to $20). Current monthly fee per customer is $40 and they have 10M customers. How many additional customers does Company A need to acquire to recover the investment in 3 years, and should they start the free service?
questions.guidance: Structure the equation comparing current profit stream vs. new profit stream net of CAPEX. Solve for additional customers X. Then assess feasibility by asking about market share and growth rate. Conclude that acquiring 40% more customers in 3 years (roughly 10% per year) far exceeds the market growth rate of 2%, making this unrealistic. Company A should consider differentiating from Company C rather than simply matching the free 3G offer.

math.setup: Current annual profit per customer = ($40 - $15) x 12 = $300. Over 3 years for 10M customers = $300 x 3 x 10M = $9,000M. New annual profit per customer = ($40 - $20) x 12 = $240. Over 3 years for (10M + X) customers minus CAPEX = $240 x 3 x (10M + X) - $1,080M. Set equal to current 3-year profit to find breakeven additional customers X.
steps: Current 3-year profit: ($40 - $15) x 12 x 3 x 10M = $25 x 12 x 3 x 10M = $9,000M
Set new profit equal to current profit: $720 x (10M + X) - $1,080M = $9,000M
math.answer: Company A needs 4M additional customers (a 40% increase from 10M) to recover the $1,080M CAPEX within 3 years.

questions.prompt: Is it realistic for Company A to acquire 4M additional customers in 3 years? Additional information: Company A has 35% market share and is the 2nd largest player; the largest player has 40% market share; UK mobile telecom market growth rate is 2%.
questions.guidance: Acquiring 40% more customers in 3 years requires approximately 10% customer growth per year. This far exceeds the UK market growth rate of 2%. Because Company C has already started the free 3G service, Company A would need to take customers from competitors — but that is extremely difficult given the competitive dynamics. The conclusion should be NO, it is not realistic. An excellent candidate will also suggest that Company A should consider a differentiated strategy (e.g., bundling 3G service with premium data content at some cost) rather than matching Company C's free offer.

recommendation: For the partnership structure: Company A should pursue a Business Alliance with Company B, paying a usage fee for 3G technology. This provides flexibility without requiring a costly acquisition or complex JV structure, and is appropriate given the limited scope of synergies.

For the free 3G service question: Company A should NOT simply match Company C's free 3G service. The required 40% customer growth in 3 years is far beyond the 2% market growth rate and is not achievable organically.
risks: If Company A does nothing in response to Company C's free 3G service, it may lose customers to Company C.
A Business Alliance gives Company A limited control over Company B's technology roadmap and service quality.
Market growth of 2% means the mobile telecom market is near saturation, limiting new customer acquisition.
next_steps: Explore a differentiated strategy — e.g., combining 3G service with exclusive data content or premium features — rather than offering it for free.
Negotiate favorable terms in the Business Alliance with Company B to allow for future escalation to a JV or M&A if strategic synergies emerge.
Conduct deeper market analysis on customer willingness-to-pay for enhanced 3G data services versus free basic service.
